title: Sumit Nagal Ends a Two-Year Title Drought in Romania. India's No. 1 Says He Questioned Everything.
excerpt: The 28-year-old from Haryana, who fell from world No. 68 to No. 297, beat France's Felix Balshaw in the Intaro Open final for his seventh Challenger title. He says the hardest battle was against himself.
body:
The win came at ten on a Sunday night in Romania, in a town most tennis fans could not locate on a map. But for Sumit Nagal, beating Felix Balshaw 6-3, 7-5 in the final of the Intaro Open in Targu Mures was about far more than the trophy. It was proof that two years of doubt, injury and ranking freefall had not broken him.

"There were times when I didn't stay motivated," Nagal told *The Bridge* after the match. "I'll be honest. I had a lot of bad thoughts. I questioned myself — what am I doing, why am I playing? Things weren't working on the court or off it."

## The numbers tell the story

In July 2024, Nagal stood at a career-high world No. 68 — the kind of ranking that earns direct entry into every Grand Slam, that puts you on Centre Court, that makes sponsors pick up the phone. He was the Indian man furthest into the tennis establishment since Somdev Devvarman's prime.

By February 2026, he had cratered to No. 297. Injuries took their toll. Results dried up. The gap between the Challenger circuit and the ATP Tour, always punishing for players from countries without deep tennis infrastructure, started to look permanent.

The Intaro Open title, his seventh on the Challenger circuit, has nudged him back to No. 219. It is not the top 100. It is not a Grand Slam main draw. But it is a direction — and for Nagal, direction matters more than destination right now.



> **""There were times when I didn't stay motivated," Nagal told *The Bridge* after the match."**


## A career built in transit

Nagal's story is, in many ways, a diaspora story. Born in Jhajjar, Haryana, to a schoolteacher father, he was plucked at age ten for Mahesh Bhupathi's Apollo Tyres Mission 2008 programme and sent to Bengaluru. When the programme folded, he moved to Toronto to train under coach Bobby Mahal. He has since been based in Germany under Sascha Nensel, with most of his competitive life spent on the European clay-court Challenger circuit.


![Targu Mures — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/4/4f/Mures_County_Prefecture.JPG)


He is 28 years old, and he has never had the luxury of a stable home base, a deep support staff, or the kind of funding that his European and American peers take for granted. Every ranking point has been earned the hard way — on budget flights, in anonymous hotels, on courts where the crowd consists mostly of other players' coaches.

## India's thin bench

Nagal is currently India's No. 1 men's singles player. Behind him, the picture is sparse. Aryan Giri sits at No. 392, Karan Singh at No. 401. The gap between India's top player and the world's elite remains vast — Jannik Sinner, the world No. 1, is currently cruising through Wimbledon's third round while Nagal was not in the main draw.

The All India Tennis Association has long been criticised for under-investing in developmental infrastructure, and the contrast with India's cricket machine — which can afford to leave Virat Kohli on the bench in a foreign T20 league — is stark. Nagal competes alone, funded largely by himself and a handful of personal sponsors.

## The road from here

Nagal's schedule for the coming weeks includes the Genesis Trading Cup and qualifying rounds at the Tulln Challenger. He needs to defend points from his 2024 run — a difficult task when you are rebuilding rather than peaking. But the Romania title provides something the rankings cannot fully capture: belief.

"It was tough to sleep on Sunday night," Nagal said. "I probably slept around 4 a.m. Winning this title is a good confidence booster. It gives me new hope and a base from which I can start pushing again."

For the small but devoted community of Indian tennis followers — and for the Indian diaspora fans who remember him as the teenager who took a set off Roger Federer at the 2019 US Open — hope has always been the commodity in shortest supply. Nagal, at least, has found some more of it.

*Sources: The Bridge, IndiaSportsHub, ATP Tour*
